questions.prompt: Using the model for The Thermodynamic Limit and Macroscopic Descriptions, set up the governing equation, inequality, derivative, probability, or phase-rule count and solve the following problem: Why do individual raindrops sound obvious on a tiny roof but blend into a steady noise on a large roof?
questions.answer:
Model:
Apply the model for The Thermodynamic Limit and Macroscopic Descriptions under every condition stated in the question; use SI units unless another unit is explicitly supplied.

Working:
Only a few drops hit the tiny roof at once, so each impact noticeably changes the total force. Many drops hit the large roof at once, and unusually large and small impacts average one another out. The large roof experiences a greater total force, but that force varies by a much smaller fraction of its average value. Final result: large numbers smooth out random variation.

Final answer:
Large numbers smooth out random variation.

Check:
The conclusion agrees with both the defining relation and the relevant limiting or qualitative behaviour of the model.

questions.answer:
Model:
Think about raindrops landing on a roof. On a tiny roof you hear separate drops, but on a huge roof the impacts blend into a nearly steady sound. Gas particles behave in the same way: individual collisions are random, but billions of billions of collisions produce steady measurements.

This is the thermodynamic limit: not the claim that a real sample is infinite, but the useful approximation that it contains enough particles for small random fluctuations to be ignored.
